body:
Energy efficiency in transport

Transport efficiency concerns the energy required to move people or goods. It depends on vehicle technology, operating conditions, occupancy or loading, route conditions and the mode of transport.

Useful comparison measures include energy per passenger-kilometre for passenger transport and energy per tonne-kilometre for freight. These measures are more informative than total vehicle fuel consumption when the amount of transport service differs.

An almost empty bus may use more energy per passenger-kilometre than the same bus carrying many passengers. Similarly, comparing the electricity consumed by an electric vehicle with the fuel consumed by another vehicle requires attention to the energy units and the distance travelled.

Ways transport systems reduce energy demand

  • Vehicle efficiency: improved motors, engines and drivetrains reduce energy losses.
  • Operational efficiency: suitable speed, maintenance, route planning and reduced unnecessary idling can lower energy use.
  • Public and shared transport: greater passenger occupancy can reduce energy use per person for a given journey, depending on the service and vehicle.
  • Freight efficiency: improved loading and appropriate use of rail or other suitable transport modes can reduce energy per tonne-kilometre.

An electric vehicle does not produce tailpipe emissions during electric operation. However, emissions associated with electricity generation and vehicle manufacture may still occur. Consequently, zero tailpipe emissions and zero lifecycle emissions are different claims.

What demand response means

Demand response means changing electricity consumption in response to a price, incentive, contractual instruction or power-system condition.

Suppose electricity demand is high during the evening. A facility that can move some water pumping to an earlier or later period may reduce its contribution to the evening peak without reducing the total amount of water pumped.

Similarly, an electric-vehicle owner may charge during a less congested period where suitable charging arrangements, tariffs or incentives exist. Such flexibility can help the grid meet demand with fewer peak-period constraints.

Peak shaving and load shifting

Peak shaving reduces the highest demand during a period. Load shifting moves some consumption from one period to another.

Both can help the electricity system, but their effects on total energy differ. If an appliance uses the same electricity before and after shifting, its total kWh consumption may remain almost unchanged even though its peak contribution falls.

Price-based and incentive-based response

Time-of-use tariffs charge different electricity prices during specified periods and can encourage consumers to alter consumption voluntarily. Other programmes may provide payments or other incentives for verified demand adjustments.

Demand-response participation depends on the relevant regulatory framework, metering arrangements and the consumer's ability to modify operations without unacceptable disruption.

Why timing matters for renewable electricity

Solar PV output is concentrated in daylight hours, whereas demand may remain high after sunset. Where feasible, shifting flexible activities toward periods of abundant generation can improve use of available electricity and reduce the need for some peak-period resources.

Demand response must not be confused with compulsory power cuts. Planned, voluntary or contractually agreed load adjustments are different from emergency load shedding imposed to maintain system security.

Prelims focus

  • Transport efficiency can be compared using energy per passenger-kilometre or per tonne-kilometre.
  • An electric vehicle has no tailpipe emissions during electric operation, but lifecycle emissions may remain.
  • Demand response changes the amount or timing of electricity use.
  • Peak shaving reduces maximum demand; load shifting moves consumption between time periods.
  • Time-of-use tariffs can encourage electricity use outside expensive or stressed periods.
  • Trap: Shifting electricity use from evening to afternoon does not necessarily reduce total kWh consumption.

[Sources: Bureau of Energy Efficiency, Energy Efficiency in Transport Sector, updated 10 August 2026; International Energy Agency, The Value of Demand Flexibility, 23 December 2025, sections on system benefits and flexible demand; International Energy Agency, Energy Transitions Require Innovation in Power System Planning, discussion of demand response, consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Efficient Transport and Demand Response: Using Energy and Electricity at the Right Time

body:
Why actual energy savings may differ from expected savings

An efficient technology can reduce the energy needed for a particular service. However, its lower operating cost may encourage people to use that service more. As a result, actual energy savings may be smaller than the savings calculated by assuming unchanged use.

The rebound effect occurs when behavioural or economic responses to improved energy efficiency offset part of the energy savings that would otherwise have been expected.

Direct and indirect rebound effects

Direct rebound occurs when the improved service itself is used more. A household may install a more efficient air conditioner but then operate it for additional hours because cooling becomes less expensive.

Indirect rebound occurs when money saved through an efficiency improvement is spent on other goods or activities that require energy. For example, reduced electricity expenditure may leave additional money for another energy-consuming activity.

EffectHow it happensIllustration
Expected technical savingThe same service needs less energy.An efficient lamp uses fewer watts for comparable lighting.
Direct reboundThe improved service is used more.The efficient lamp is left on for longer.
Indirect reboundFinancial savings support other energy-consuming activities.Money saved on lighting is spent on additional travel.

A simple rebound calculation

Suppose a technical improvement is expected to reduce energy consumption from 100 kWh to 60 kWh for unchanged service. The expected saving is 40 kWh. If the user increases consumption of the service and actual use becomes 70 kWh, the realised saving is 30 kWh.

The additional 10 kWh offsets 10 kWh of the expected 40 kWh saving. In this illustration, the direct rebound amounts to 25% of the expected saving.

Rebound effects vary across technologies, households, industries and economic conditions. They should not be assumed to occur at one fixed percentage.

Does greater efficiency always increase total energy use?

No. The usual rebound-effect concept describes a reduction in expected savings, not necessarily an increase in total energy consumption. Under some conditions, additional energy use could exceed the expected saving; this is called backfire. It is a possible outcome, not an automatic consequence of efficiency improvements.

The historical idea commonly associated with Jevons' paradox concerns situations in which improvements in the efficiency of resource use contribute to greater overall consumption of that resource. It should not be interpreted as a universal rule that efficiency measures are ineffective.

When an underserved household uses the lower operating cost of efficient equipment to obtain more cooling or lighting, the result may improve welfare even if measured energy savings are smaller than originally estimated. Energy access, useful service and total consumption should therefore be evaluated separately.

Connecting the electricity system with energy efficiency

The electricity system and energy efficiency influence each other. Efficient buildings, pumps, appliances and industrial processes reduce the energy required to provide useful services. This can lower the amount of electricity that must be generated and delivered.

Reducing peak demand can also ease pressure on generators, transmission corridors and distribution equipment. Demand response adds another option by moving flexible consumption toward times when electricity and network capacity are more readily available.

However, neither efficiency nor demand response replaces the need for reliable generation, secure transmission, functioning distribution networks and competent system operation.

Final conceptual distinctions

  • Generation versus transmission: electricity is produced at generating facilities and transferred through networks.
  • Transmission versus distribution: bulk power transfer differs from local consumer supply.
  • Power versus energy: kW measures a rate; kWh measures an amount accumulated over time.
  • Frequency versus voltage: grid frequency reflects overall AC power balance; voltage is electrical potential difference.
  • Technical versus commercial loss: physical energy dissipation differs from measurement, billing and collection failures.
  • Energy efficiency versus demand response: using less energy for the same service differs from changing the timing or level of demand in response to system conditions.
  • Renewable generation versus efficiency: changing the energy source differs from reducing energy input per unit of useful output.
  • Technical saving versus realised saving: behavioural changes can reduce the savings achieved after an efficiency improvement.

Prelims focus

  • Direct rebound concerns additional use of the newly efficient service.
  • Indirect rebound concerns additional energy use through spending or other economic responses.
  • Rebound can reduce expected energy savings without eliminating them.
  • Backfire describes a case in which rebound more than offsets the expected saving.
  • Electricity-system reliability requires generation, networks, protection and coordinated operation.
  • Trap: An efficiency improvement does not guarantee an equal percentage reduction in total electricity consumption when usage patterns change.

[Sources: International Energy Agency, Capturing the Multiple Benefits of Energy Efficiency, 2014, section The Rebound Effect in a Multiple Benefits Context; International Energy Agency, Efficiency Should Always Be the First Answer, discussion of rebound effects and energy-service access; United States Department of Energy, Appendix 10E: Rebound Effect Analysis, 2023, sections 10E.1–10E.2; International Energy Agency, The Value of Demand Flexibility, 2025, consulted 16 November 2026.]
